pub_kaplan2020_fig1_scaling_laws.png: Published figure: Figure 1 of Kaplan et al. (2020), Scaling laws for neural language models. Three side-by-side line plots, each with both axes on a logarithmic scale and the language model's test loss (cross-entropy, from about 2 to 7) on the vertical axis. Left panel: loss against compute in petaflop-days, from 10 to the minus 9 up to 10, drawn as many pale blue training curves with a black lower envelope and an orange dashed power-law fit, loss = (compute / 2.3 times 10 to the 8) to the power minus 0.050. Middle panel: loss against dataset size in tokens, from about 2 times 10 to the 7 to 2 times 10 to the 9, with six blue points falling from about 4.1 to 2.7 along a grey line with exponent minus 0.095. Right panel: loss against non-embedding parameters, from about 10 to the 3 to 10 to the 9, with many points falling from about 5.6 to 2.3 along a grey line with exponent minus 0.076. On a log-log plot a power law is a straight line, and all three are straight over several orders of magnitude. The slide uses this to show that loss falls smoothly and predictably as compute, data or parameters grow.
s22_img01.png: Published figure from Brown et al. (2020), the GPT-3 paper, showing accuracy on a word-unscrambling task against the number of examples placed in the prompt. The horizontal axis is the number of examples in context, 0 at the left, then 1 and 10 on a logarithmic scale; labels above mark zero-shot (no examples), one-shot (one example) and few-shot (many). The vertical axis is accuracy in percent, 0 to about 67. Three colored groups of lines are labeled 175B, 13B and 1.3B parameters; for each size a solid line is a prompt that also describes the task in natural language and a dashed line has no such description. The 175-billion-parameter model starts at about 8 percent with no examples, reaches about 46 percent with one example when the task is described (about 26 without), and climbs to about 67 percent. The 13-billion model rises from about 1 to about 25 percent, and the 1.3-billion model stays below 5 percent. The task description helps mostly when examples are few. The slide uses the figure to show that in-context learning improves with model size and with more examples.
real_icl.svg: Real computation on three small public models, GPT-2 small (124 million parameters), medium (355 million) and large (774 million). A line plot with solid points joined by lines. The horizontal axis is the number of solved examples in the prompt, at 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8. The vertical axis is the percentage of antonym questions answered correctly, 0 to 100. The prompt is a list of word pairs such as hot, cold, followed by a new word whose opposite the model must produce. GPT-2 small stays low at every count, peaking at about 10 percent with one example and sliding to about 4 percent at eight. GPT-2 medium rises from 0 to about 22, 64, 88 and 94 percent. GPT-2 large rises from about 4 to 25, 81, 92 and 96 percent. The two larger models nearly coincide by eight examples. No weights change in any of these runs; only the prompt grows. The slide uses this to show that in-context learning appears with scale and improves with examples, using models students can run themselves.
pub_brown2020_fig1_1_meta_learning.png: Published diagram: Figure 1.1 of Brown et al. (2020), the GPT-3 paper, a schematic of language-model meta-learning with two nested loops. The outer loop is learning by stochastic gradient descent during pretraining, which runs over many text sequences. Inside each sequence is an inner loop of in-context learning, a list of examples of one task followed by a new case the model must complete. Three example sequences are shown: addition, such as 5 + 8 = 13 and 7 + 2 = 9, then a new sum; unscrambling words, such as gaot => goat, then a new scrambled word; and translating English to French, such as thanks => merci, then a new word. The point is that the model learns, across training, to pick up a task from the examples in its own context. The slide uses this to name in-context learning as a skill acquired by pretraining on text, with no weight update at test time.
pub_ouyang2022_fig2_rlhf_steps.png: Published diagram: Figure 2 of Ouyang et al. (2022), the InstructGPT paper, showing three training steps as three panels from left to right. Step 1, supervised fine-tuning: a prompt such as Explain the moon landing to a 6 year old is given to a human labeler, who writes a good answer; GPT-3 is fine-tuned on these demonstrations. Step 2, reward model: the model writes several answers to a prompt, a labeler ranks them from best to worst, and the rankings train a reward model that scores answers. Step 3, reinforcement learning: for a new prompt such as Write a story about frogs, the model writes an answer, the reward model scores it, and that score updates the model with a policy-gradient method (PPO). Arrows connect prompts, outputs, labelers and models. The slide uses it to show how a pretrained next-token predictor becomes an assistant that follows instructions.
real_surprisal.svg: Real computation on three public models, GPT-2 small (124 million parameters), medium (355 million) and large (774 million). A grouped bar chart. The horizontal axis lists the tokens of the sentence My grandmother's recipe calls for two cups of flour and a pinch of salt, with a leading space marked by a dot; the first token has no bar because nothing precedes it. Each token has three bars, one per model, giving its surprisal in bits, the negative base-2 log probability the model gave it given the earlier words, on a vertical axis running 0 to about 15. Grandmother is the tallest, 14.5 bits for the small model (a callout says about 1 chance in 22,657) and about 8.5 for the medium and large ones. Recipe is about 8 to 10 bits. The token for and the second of are near zero, and a callout notes that 0 bits means the model was sure. Salt is also near zero. Mean surprisal over the sentence is 4.0, 3.5 and 3.3 bits for small, medium and large. The slide uses this to show what surprisal is and that bigger models are on average less surprised.
real_reading_times.svg: Real data and computation on one sentence from the Natural Stories self-paced reading corpus, Seeds from a tulip will form a flowering bulb after seven-twelve years. Two stacked bar charts share the same twelve words along the bottom. The top chart gives mean reading time in milliseconds, 0 to about 900, averaged over many readers. Most words sit between about 310 and 500 ms (Seeds about 490, a about 310). Seven-twelve, drawn in red, is about 580 ms, and the final word years is the slowest at about 870 ms. The bottom chart gives each word's surprisal in bits under GPT-2 small, 0 to about 25. Most words are 2 to 10 bits (flowering about 10, the second a about 2), while seven-twelve, also in red, is the clear peak at about 25 bits. The unexpected word draws the highest surprisal and a longer reading time, and the slowdown carries into the next word. The slide uses this to link model surprisal to human reading times.
pub_oh2023_fig1_natural_stories.png: Published figure: Figure 1 of Oh and Schuler (2023), panel for the Natural Stories self-paced reading corpus. A scatter plot. The horizontal axis is language-model perplexity on a log scale, from about 2 to the 3.2 to 2 to the 4.8; the vertical axis is delta log-likelihood, the gain in how well a regression predicts human reading times when the model's surprisal is added, from about 375 to 640. Three model families are plotted with dashed least-squares lines: GPT-2 (blue circles, small to XL), GPT-Neo (orange squares, 125 million to 20 billion parameters) and OPT (green hexagons, 125 million to 66 billion). Each point is labeled with its size. In every family the smallest models, with the highest perplexity, give the largest gain, near 600 to 640, and the largest models give the smallest, near 380 to 400. Better next-word predictors therefore explain reading times worse. The slide uses this to show that the best language model is not the best model of human reading.
pub_tuckute2024_fig2_drive_suppress.png: Published figure: Figure 2 of Tuckute et al. (2024), driving and suppressing the human language network with sentences chosen by a language model. Panel A shows the left hemisphere on an inflated brain, with the language network in red along the temporal lobe and in frontal cortex, defined separately for each participant. Panel B is a bar chart for an event-related design with three participants. Vertical axis: z-scored fMRI (BOLD) response of the language network; bars for the drive, suppress and baseline conditions. Drive sentences are highest at about 0.28, suppress sentences are lowest at about minus 0.29, and baseline is near 0; dots show individuals. Panel C is the same for a blocked design with four participants: drive about 0.7, suppress about minus 1.2, baseline about 0.5. Panel D lists example sentences. Drive sentences are odd or fragmentary, such as Jiffy Lube of -- of therapies, yes. Suppress sentences are plain, such as We were sitting on the couch. Baseline sentences are ordinary corpus text. The slide uses this to show that a model of language can predict, and control, activity in the brain's language regions.
pub_caucheteux2023_fig2_forecast.png: Published figure: Figure 2 of Caucheteux, Gramfort and King (2023), evidence for predictive coding in the brain during language comprehension. Seven panels labeled a to g, from fMRI of 304 people listening to stories. Panel a, brain maps: the brain score of GPT-2 activations, how well they predict each region's activity, from 0.005 to 0.230, is highest along the superior temporal sulcus. Panels b and d, line plots: adding the model's representation of the word d positions ahead (horizontal axis, distance to the current word, minus 10 to 30) raises the brain score, peaking at about 8 words ahead. Panel c, brain map: the regions where this forecast gain is significant, across temporal, parietal and frontal cortex. Panel e, brain map: the best forecast distance in each region, from 7.5 to 9.5 words. Panel f, line plots comparing two regions: forecast score peaks earlier in anterior superior temporal sulcus (about 7 words) than in inferior frontal gyrus (about 9). Panel g, dots by region, show best forecast distance growing from about 8 in the mid superior temporal sulcus to about 9.2 in frontal regions. The slide uses this to show that the brain appears to predict upcoming words, further ahead in higher regions.
figure1_cropped.png: Published diagram: Figure 1 of Lotter, Kreiman and Cox (2016), the PredNet architecture. Left side: two stacked layers, l and l plus 1. Each layer has four kinds of square module. Green representation units R, with a recurrent loop arrow, send a prediction down to a blue module (A-hat), the predicted input. This is compared, through a circled minus sign, with a blue target module A, the actual input of that layer. The difference feeds a red error module E. Error signals go up the hierarchy to the next layer's target and to the representation units, and the representation of the higher layer passes downward to the one below. Right side: the same unit drawn with its operations. Representation is a convolutional LSTM; the prediction is a convolution; the target is a convolution then pooling of the input; and the error subtracts the two and applies a rectifier to the positive and negative parts. The slide uses this to show a network built around predicting its input and passing on only the error.
